To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the data are consistent with a partial dissipation or a gaussian mean-temperature-profile model with a thermal width equal to about 1/2 of the mean turbulent front radius, with the rms temperature fluctuation on the axis equal to about 0.5 times the mean wake temperature, and the mixing-lag time equal to about 40 wake radii.

the partial dissipation or "bimodal" model is the only model that is consistent with the observed radiation and the observed temperature fluctuations, that the turbulent temperature and mass fluctuations are about the same, that the rms temperature fluctuation on the axis is about 30 percent of the mean, that the mixing-lags are about 20 wake-radii, and that the mean temperature profile is Gaussian.
the partial dissipation or "bimodal" model is consistent with the O2 chemiluminescence radiation measurements behind a sphere in air in the GM Ballistic Range.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of temperature fluctuations on a chemical reaction in a hypersonic, turbulent wake.

the effects of turbulent fluctuations of temperature in a hypersonic wake on the radiation of a chemical species with a strong temperature sensitivity, and the results are used to deduce the turbulence parameters.
the interpretation of experimental measurements of turbulent fluctuations of temperature, mass density, and electron density in hypersonic wakes in terms of various turbulent wake models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the partial dissipation or the bimodal model with an unmixed volume fraction equal to 0.1 is the best model for the wake.
the partial dissipation or "bimodal" model is the most satisfactory model to explain the observed O2 recombination chemiluminescence behind a hypersonic sphere.
the data are consistent with the Gaussian mean-tem-perature profile with fluctuations and that the partial dissipation and the mixing-lag models are consistent with the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the partial dissipation or "bimodal" model is the best model for the wake, with the mixing-lag model being the second best.
the data can best be explained by a model which involves a partial dissipation of turbulence in the turbulent wake, and a gaussian mean-temperature wake profile with superimposition of fluctuations.
the partial dissipation, mixing-lag, and Gaussian models are all consistent with the radiation data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the turbulent wake models a, b and d are inconsistent, and the mixing-lag models are not applicable to wakes in which the mixing-lag time is much longer than the chemical time scale.
the turbulent wake models are inadequate to explain the observed O sub 2 emission.

the mixing-lagged partial dissipation model is consistent with the radiation data, and the model involving the Gaussian profile is consistent with the temperature fluctuations and radiation data, but the latter model is very sensitive to the temperature profile.
